text: well as for patients with reflux oesophagitis.8 There is no evidence for the superiority of any particular PPI, nor for greater benefit from doubling doses in patients with reflux oesophagitis.7 A significant minority of patients do not, however, re- spond to PPIs; reasons may include poor compliance, noc- turnal acid breakthrough, non-acid reflux, and hypersensi- tivity to acid.4,5 Trying an alternative PPI or increasing the dose has been suggested4 (despite the lack of evidence to support this7). However, in refractory cases, giving a pro- ton pump inhibitor with an H2-antagonist may be more ef- fective than just increasing the dose of the former.4,9 Alternatively, a prokinetic drug such as metoclopramide may improve gastro-oesophageal sphincter function and accelerate gastric emptying. These appear to be as effec- tive as H2-antagonists,1 although they are probably less ef- fective than PPIs.7 An H2-antagonist used with cisapride may be more effective than either drug alone.1 However, concern over the risk of cardiotoxicity and potential for se- rious interactions with cisapride has led to severe restric- tions on its use. In patients with mild disease, a trial of withdrawal of drug therapy is appropriate after successful initial treatment.1 Short courses of therapy as and when symptoms demand (intermittent treatment) may be effective in uncomplicated disease.10 However, most patients with oesophagitis re- lapse when treatment is withdrawn, and long-term main- tenance therapy is likely to be required.1,4,5 As in acute management, PPIs appear to be the most effective mainte- nance treatment, although the ‘step-down’ approach of re- duced maintenance doses, which is widely favoured,4,5 may produce less benefit than continuing to give full dose PPIs.11 H2 antagonists were found to be of marginal bene- fit for maintenance, although they did give some sympto- matic relief, and although prokinetic drugs (cisapride) and sucralfate were also reported to be more effective than pla- cebo their value was considered dubious.11 Another ap- proach is to use a combination for maintenance, and in one study omeprazole with cisapride provided more effective maintenance than ranitidine or cisapride alone or in com- bination.12 Again, however, cisapride is now unlikely to be used in practice because of the risks.
